claims.text: CPPD is arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals; formerly called pseudogout
claims.quote: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease is arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals (). Until recently, CPPD disease has been referred to as pseudogout.

claims.text: acute pseudogout attack can be indistinguishable from gout or joint infection; warmth, redness, swelling
claims.quote: The vigorous inflammatory response to CPP crystals manifests as warmth, erythema, and swelling in and around the affected joint, and the clinical picture is often indistinguishable from acute gouty arthritis or septic arthritis.

claims.text: knee most common, then wrist; acute big-toe attack rare
claims.quote: The knee is the most commonly involved joint, followed by the wrist; acute podagra in the first metatarsophalangeal joint is rare.

claims.text: chronic CPPD favors shoulder, wrist and MCP joints
claims.quote: The involvement of joints such as the glenohumeral joint, the wrist, and the metacarpophalangeal joints, which are not often affected by typical osteoarthritis, should lead one to suspect the presence of CPPD disease

claims.text: fever and chills can occur with a pseudogout attack
claims.quote: Systemic symptoms including fevers, chills, and constitutional symptoms often occur with acute CPP crystal arthritis.

claims.text: pseudogout attacks may last weeks to months, longer than gout attacks
claims.quote: In contrast to the brief attacks of acute gouty arthritis that typically last for several days to 1 week, acute attacks of CPPD disease may last for weeks to months.

claims.text: CPP crystals form in cartilage; rarely form outside cartilage
claims.quote: the formation of CPP crystals in the pericellular matrix of cartilage is the essential first step in the disease process (). CPP crystals rarely form in noncartilaginous tissues.

claims.text: pyrophosphate plays a role in CPPD analogous to urate in gout (not driven by urate)
claims.quote: Inorganic pyrophosphate plays a central role in CPPD that is analogous to that of urate in gout and may be a key therapeutic target.

claims.text: rare before 60; X-ray chondrocalcinosis doubles each decade over 60; 44% over 84
claims.quote: rare in patients younger than 60 years of age. ... chondrocalcinosis is detected in 44% of patients older than 84 years of age; the prevalence doubles with each decade over 60 years of age.

claims.text: joint injury raises risk
claims.quote: Previous trauma to the joint is also a strong risk factor for CPPD.

claims.text: associations: hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatasia; screening especially under 60
claims.quote: CPPD disease can be a presenting sign of hyperparathyroidism, hypophosphatasia, hemochromatosis, or hypomagnesemia. Screening is indicated for these conditions, particularly in patients younger than 60 years of age who present with CPPD disease.

claims.text: up to 5% of people with gout have CPP crystals in joint fluid (coexistence)
claims.quote: As many as 5% of patients with gout have CPP crystals in their synovial fluid,which supports the hypothesis that these diseases share common local and systemic risk factors.

claims.text: screening blood tests: iron studies, calcium, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone
claims.quote: We recommend iron studies, including measurement of iron, transferrin, and ferritin levels, as well as measurement of levels of serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone.

claims.text: attacks follow acute illness, joint injury, surgery; no known dietary associations
claims.quote: Acute attacks of CPPD disease often occur in the context of acute illness or joint trauma or in the postoperative period, particularly after parathyroidectomyor hip-fracture repair.There are no known dietary associations of CPPD disease.

claims.text: CPP crystals positively birefringent, rhomboid; often weakly birefringent
claims.quote: CPPD disease is most accurately diagnosed by the finding of positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped crystals in synovial fluid from the affected joint (). ... these crystals are small and often show weak birefringence.

claims.text: red-filter color pattern: CPP blue parallel/yellow perpendicular; urate opposite
claims.quote: CPP crystals appear blue when they are parallel to the axis of the polarizer and yellow when they are perpendicular. In contrast, monosodium urate crystals appear yellow when they are parallel ... and blue when they are perpendicular.

claims.text: diagnosis confirmed by crystals; joint pattern is a clue
claims.quote: Along with other findings, the distribution of joint involvement may provide a helpful clue with regard to the presence of acute CPP crystal arthritis.

claims.text: chondrocalcinosis on X-ray supports but does not replace crystal diagnosis
claims.quote: Although chondrocalcinosis is the radiographic finding that is most closely aligned with CPPD disease, it should not be used as a sole diagnostic criterion in the absence of clinical arthritis.

claims.text: acute treatment: intra-articular steroid often first-line; colchicine, NSAIDs, systemic steroids alternatives
claims.quote: Intraarticular glucocorticoids work well for patients with acute CPP crystal arthritis, and this treatment is typically recommended as first-line therapy for joints that are amenable to injection.

claims.text: NSAIDs and systemic glucocorticoids used for acute flares
claims.quote: Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), given at antiinflammatory daily doses and preferably used along with gastroprotection, may be effective for treating acute flares. Systemic glucocorticoids are also frequently used

claims.text: no urate-lowering or disease-modifying drug for CPPD
claims.quote: Unlike the case with gout, in which long-term therapies reduce the urate burden, no current disease-modulating treatments are available for CPPD disease.

claims.text: low-dose colchicine may reduce recurrences
claims.quote: The daily use of oral colchicine at a low dose (0.6 to 1.2 mg) may be useful in reducing the frequency of acute attacks.

claims.text: rare tumor-like soft tissue CPP deposits (tophi FAQ)
claims.quote: Rarely, tumoral deposits of CPP crystals occur in soft tissues, where they can cause considerable tissue damage and may be mistaken for cancers.

claims.text: fever with a hot joint should not be assumed to be crystal arthritis without evaluation (fever can occur in pseudogout; picture indistinguishable from septic arthritis)
claims.quote: the clinical picture is often indistinguishable from acute gouty arthritis or septic arthritis.
